attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own newsletter, stated as his analysis.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the five named exclusions, the three companies and the 'barely $1 billion' threshold. It is a present-tense observation, not a forecast.

contract.note: Reading it as a 2025 calendar-year estimate, excluding exactly the five named customers, is fair and ordinary given the context. Treating 'barely' as roughly $1B or less is reasonable. The result depends on how revenue is allocated by customer, which the speaker did not supply.

evidence.note: CoreWeave's FY25 10-K (available 2026-03) gives Microsoft about 67% of revenue and says no other customer reached 10%. The excerpt has no total and no amounts for Nvidia, Google or OpenAI, so the residual cannot be computed.
Nebius defines ARR as an annualized measure, not earned annual revenue, and gives no customer allocation. It cannot settle the residual.

reviews.rationale: Testing this needs, for each of the three firms, 2025 revenue minus the amounts from the five named customers. The packet has only CoreWeave's Microsoft share plus a 10% ceiling for other customers, and Nebius ARR definitions. Nothing for Lambda. No defensible bounds show the residual is near $1B or well above it, so the evidence does not settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own essay.

semantics.note: Faithful to the sentence and the premises just before it. But the claim only says the savings are uncertain; it does not commit to the router saving or losing money.

contract.note: Fairly treats 'unclear' as an expression of uncertainty with no testable outcome. The premises about compute and caching are correctly left ungraded.

evidence.note: The Register (Aug 2025) describes the router's savings only 'in theory', with no figures from OpenAI. This fits the uncertainty but settles no factual point.

reviews.rationale: Saying it is 'unclear' whether the router saves money commits the speaker to no definite outcome. It is an expression of uncertainty, which is not scored under policy. The packet is consistent with no public router-level cost data, but no finding is possible.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion. He derives the revenue from a report in The Information, but he endorses both the figure and the claim that it is unprofitable.

semantics.note: Keeps both parts: about $33M a month (July run rate divided by 12) and 'all of it unprofitable'. Leaving out the impressionistic 'ubiquitous' clause is right.

contract.note: Fair plain reading. It ties the figure to the July 2025 run rate, as the context does, and requires product-level evidence that costs exceeded revenue for 'unprofitable'.

evidence.note: TechCrunch (Nov 2025) reports Claude Code at about $400M annualized in July, which is about $33M a month. This supports the revenue part only and says nothing on product profitability.

reviews.rationale: The revenue part holds: about $400M annualized in July is about $33M a month. The substantive part, 'all of it unprofitable', has no product-level cost or profit evidence in the packet, and company-wide losses cannot establish it. The support condition needs both parts, so the claim as a whole is not settled.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sweeping statement in his own essay.

semantics.note: Faithful to the three-part universal claim. Dropping the 'I've been saying so' self-reference is correct. 'Reliable' and 'sustainable' are largely rhetorical, with no measure given.

contract.note: The sector-wide plain reading is ordinary, and a single provider exception is rightly not decisive. But reliability thresholds, sector boundary and what 'sustainability' means all have to be supplied by the evaluator, so interpretation drives the result.

evidence.note: A September 2025 factuality benchmark shows limits on one narrow task. It is not a measure of reliability across ordinary uses or over the whole history.
Midjourney's founder reported profitability in 2022. This is a company's self-report; it challenges an exceptionless reading but does not establish sector-wide profitability.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no sector-wide profit series, no defined reliability test across ordinary uses, and no sustainability measure. A narrow benchmark and one self-reported profitable provider cannot settle a sector-level reading in either direction, so the claim stays unresolved.
